book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would start with Bretton Woods as a dated institution and list fixed vs floating regimes. The video starts from the learner's last lesson (devaluation helps exports), asks the questions that lesson left open, and goes into history to answer them. It then splits the system into two named sub-questions (what 'fixed to gold' means, what 'pegging' means), answers each with a moving picture, names the regime only after showing all currencies tied together, and makes the regime concrete with a running character buying an imported car. Devaluation is then shown as the central bank's lever inside that same money path, and the collapse closes the loop on the gold link stated at the start.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Break a system statement into its named parts (fixed to gold, pegged to dollar), teach each part with one moving picture and a small number, then run one concrete transaction through the whole system and change one number to show the lever.

talmel_summary: The middle of the video is the strongest fit: gold equals dollar with root-like PEGGED arrows, the rupee hung from the dollar on a rod riding a rising line, a ±1% chip for the crawling peg, then the importer's money visibly travelling to the bank, to RBI and out of the reserve stack, and a new rate card dropping under the old one at the devaluation. The opening recap boxes appear 2-3 s before their words, which works because the chain is familiar. Weak spots: the humour caricature and question fill a gap with no teaching, the BoP crisis exists only on screen, and the collapse is a text box plus a cross while the voice gives a long, fast explanation.

voice.notes: About 190 words per minute, quick and steady. Uses fixed explaining phrases: 'dekhiye', 'iska matlab yeh hua', 'maan lijiye', 'chaliye', 'gaur karne wali baat yeh hai'. Splits a statement aloud into 'do cheezein hain: pehli..., doosri...'. Numbers in Indian units ('1 lakh dollars', '3.3 lakh rupees'), rates as '1 dollar is equal to 4.76 rupees'. One humour line ('yeh ek bahut lambi kahani hai') in a playful tone. The collapse explanation near the end runs as one long unbroken sentence.

game_ideas.player_does: Holds the rupee on a rod under the moving dollar: picks a hard peg (rate locked at 5) or a crawling peg (±1% band) and responds as market pushes nudge the rupee up and down while gold drags the dollar along a rising line.
game_ideas.process_happens: The rate card shows the live rate; under a hard peg the rod is rigid, under a crawling peg the pin slides inside a yellow band.
game_ideas.win: Keep the rate inside the allowed band for ten ticks while the dollar moves.
game_ideas.lose: Letting the rupee drift outside the band snaps the rod and the rate card turns red, showing the peg has broken.

game_ideas.player_does: Plays RBI at the dollar window under a fixed rate of 3.30: importers (the car buyer, a machine buyer, an oil buyer) queue with rupees asking for dollars, and RBI decides each round whether to pay out or devalue.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each payout lifts dollars off the forex reserve stack; a devaluation drops a new rate card (4.76, later 7.50) and every importer must now bring more rupees, so fewer can afford imports.
game_ideas.win: Finish ten rounds with reserves above zero and as few devaluations as possible.
game_ideas.lose: Paying out every request empties the stack and a 'balance of payment crisis' banner appears.
game_ideas.concept: how the fixed regime works and why central banks devalue

game_ideas.player_does: Links cards in order: dollar convertible into gold -> other currencies pegged to the dollar -> the system stands on this link -> US suspends convertibility -> Bretton Woods collapses -> India moves to a peg regime.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct link lights a segment of the 1944-1971 timeline; the final link drops the red cross at 1971.
game_ideas.win: Full chain lit with the cross at 1971.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the collapse before the suspension leaves the gold link standing, with a nudge that nothing has broken yet.

game_ideas.player_does: Places rate cards 3.30 (1948), 4.76 (1949), 7.50 (1966) and re-prices the 1-lakh-dollar car at each.
game_ideas.process_happens: The car's rupee tag updates (3.30 lakh, 4.76 lakh, 7.50 lakh) as each card is placed.
game_ideas.win: All three cards in order with the right car prices.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong car price shows the multiplication line with the wrong factor highlighted.
game_ideas.concept: India's devaluations and their effect on import prices

checks_learned: Questions promised in the agenda (depreciation vs devaluation, who does it) must be answered in the lesson or explicitly deferred; flag open promises at the end.
Every number on screen must be spoken (±1% is on screen; the voice says 'some percent').
Every effect named on screen must be spoken (balance of payment crisis is only on screen).
The agent on screen must match the agent in the voice (screen: government devalued; voice: central bank devalues).
After a rule change (devaluation), re-run the same running example with the new number (E19 does this with the car; enforce it).
A definition note should not appear more than about 3 s before its term (the hard-peg note leads by about 6 s).
No caricatures of real people or brand founders; BIE uses its own recurring characters.
A humour beat must not replace the bridge question's teaching; the question should still be spoken and pictured.

teaching_best.why: The rupee hangs from the dollar on a rod and rides the rising line: a peg made physical, then a ±1% chip shows the crawling peg as a small allowed band.
'Two things here' splits the system statement into two named sub-questions and answers them in that order.
A running character's car purchase turns the fixed rate into rupees and then into a money path through the bank, RBI and the reserve stack.
The same import is re-priced after devaluation (3.30 lakh to 4.76 lakh) and the rate cards line up as a history strip.
The recap is a visible cause chain, so the new question grows out of the learner's last lesson.

teaching_weak.why: Promises the depreciation vs devaluation difference, which this video never delivers.
A caricature and a joke bubble fill the bridge, with a real-person likeness BIE cannot use.
The BoP crisis and 'solution' are text only; the reserve stack never visibly runs low.
The collapse (convertibility suspended) is one long fast sentence over a text box and a cross; no picture of dollars being turned into gold.
'Gold up, dollar up' is said while the screen shows a static equation; nothing moves.
